big: Meena buys a health policy in March and is diagnosed with a heart condition in April. The claim is rejected. She is angry, but the policy had a clause she never read.

lines: I paid my premium on time. Why was my claim refused?
Most refusals come from waiting periods, exclusions and things not told at purchase. Let us check each.

title: Waiting and exclusions
stops: A new policy covers every illness from day one
Existing illnesses are covered only after a waiting period
Hiding an illness can get a claim rejected
caps: Cover for some illnesses starts only after a waiting period.
An illness you already had is covered after its own waiting period.
Not telling the insurer about it can lead to rejection.
Cosmetic and some other treatments are excluded.

intro: Under current rules the waiting for existing illnesses is capped, but plans differ. Check your policy.
rows: An illness you had before buying
Time before certain claims become payable
After five continuous years, claims cannot be contested for non-disclosure, except fraud
note: Waiting periods run from the start of the policy and restart if you move to a new insurer without porting.

q: Rohan buys a policy and develops a covered illness in week two. A 30-day initial wait applies. What happens?
opts: Usually rejected, since it falls in the initial wait
The claim is paid, since he paid the premium on time
The claim is paid half, since he waited two weeks
The insurer cancels the policy and refunds the premium
why: Illness claims in the initial wait period are usually not payable, apart from accidents.
The premium alone does not make a claim payable. The wait rules still apply.
There is no half-payment rule. The claim falls in a period where it is not payable.
The policy stays active. Only the claim in the wait period is affected.

q: Meena had diabetes before buying a policy and told the insurer. What is the likely outcome?
opts: Covered from day one, since she told the insurer about it
She cannot buy any health policy at all in India
Covered only after the pre-existing waiting period ends
All her claims are excluded forever, whatever the illness is
why: Disclosure keeps the claim honest, but the waiting period still applies.
Insurers do sell policies to people with existing conditions, usually with waiting periods.
Pre-existing illnesses are covered after a waiting period, even if disclosed.
Cover begins after the wait, and other illnesses are covered in the normal way.

q: Rohan did not mention his blood pressure when buying. A claim arises two years later. What is the risk?
opts: None, since the policy is already in force for years
The insurer must pay, since two full years have passed
The premium simply rises by a small amount at renewal
It may be rejected for non-disclosure of a material fact
why: A policy in force can still be challenged for hiding a material fact.
The moratorium protects after five continuous years, not two, and not for fraud.
The consequence can be a rejected claim, not just a higher premium.
Material facts must be disclosed, and hiding them can lead to rejection.

q: What does the moratorium period mean?
opts: A period when the premium cannot be raised for any reason at all
Continuous cover after which claims are safe, apart from fraud
The time within which a claim must be made after discharge from care
A pause in cover while the insurer checks your documents
why: It does not freeze premiums. It protects claims from being contested.
After continuous cover, claims are protected from challenge, except for fraud.
Claim filing deadlines are separate rules. This term is about contesting claims.
Cover does not pause. The term refers to protection after continuous years of cover.

pts: Cover for some illnesses starts only after a waiting period.
Tell the insurer everything that matters when you buy.
Exclusions are things the policy never covers, so read the list.
